title: The Winning of a Queen: Chapter 6
paragraphs: _How King Arthur Was Married in Royal State and How the Round Table Was Established._

Now the early fall of the year had come. It was that pleasant season when the meadows and the open country were still green with the summer that had just passed. The sky was still like summer, extraordinarily blue and full of large drifting clouds. A bird might sing here and another there, a short song in memory of spring. The air was warm, yet the leaves everywhere were turning brown and red and gold. When the sun shone through them, it was as though a cloth of gold, embroidered with brown and crimson and green, hung above your head. At this time of year it is wonderfully pleasant to be out in the fields among the nut trees with hawk and hound, or to travel through the yellow countryside, whether on horseback or on foot.

This was the time of year set for the marriage of King Arthur and the Lady Guinevere at Camelot, and the place was filled with extraordinary pomp and glory. All the world was stirring and bubbling with joy, for everyone was very glad that King Arthur was to have a Queen.

To prepare for that great occasion, the town of Camelot was decorated magnificently. The stony street along which the Lady Guinevere must travel to the King’s royal castle was strewn thickly with fresh-cut rushes, laid smooth. In many places it was also covered with carpets of excellent pattern, fit to lie on the floor of some splendid hall. All the houses along the way were hung with fine woven cloths shot through with threads of blue and crimson. Everywhere flags and banners floated in the warm, gentle breeze against the blue sky. The whole world seemed alive with bright colors, so that anyone looking down that street saw a winding path of wonderful beauty and gaiety stretched out before him.
So the King’s wedding day came—bright and clear and radiant.

King Arthur sat in his hall, surrounded by his Court, waiting for news that the Lady Guinevere was coming. About the middle of the morning, a messenger came riding in haste upon a milk-white horse. The messenger’s clothes and his horse’s trappings were all of cloth of gold embroidered with scarlet and white. His tabard was set with many jewels of different kinds, so that he glittered from far away as he rode, with a singular splendor.
This herald came straight into the castle where the King sat waiting, and he said: “Rise, my lord King, for the Lady Guinevere and her Court are drawing near.”

At this the King rose at once with great joy and went out with his Court of Knights, riding in great state. As he went down that marvelously decorated street, all the people shouted aloud as he passed by. He smiled and bowed his head from side to side, for that day he was very happy and loved his people with wonderful friendliness.

So he rode on to the town gate and out through it, and came into the countryside beyond. There the broad, well-worn highway ran winding down beside the shining river, between the willows and the osiers.

And behold! King Arthur and those with him saw the Princess’s Court far off in the distance. They rejoiced greatly and hurried forward with all speed. As they drew near, the sun fell upon the silk and cloth of gold, and upon the golden chains and the jewels that hung from them. All of that noble company surrounding the Lady Guinevere’s litter flashed and sparkled with dazzling radiance.

Seventeen of the noblest knights of the King’s Court, dressed in full armor, had been sent by him as an escort for the lady. They rode in great splendor around the litter in which the Princess lay. The frame of the litter was of richly gilded wood, and its curtains and cushions were of crimson silk embroidered with gold thread. Behind the litter rode the Princess’s Court in gay and joyful array, shining with many colors. There were her ladies-in-waiting, gentlemen, ladies, pages, and attendants.
So the King’s party and the Lady Guinevere’s party drew near to each other until they met and mingled together.

Then King Arthur at once got down from his noble horse. Dressed in all his royal robes, he went on foot to the Lady Guinevere’s litter, while Sir Gawaine and Sir Ewaine held his horse’s bridle. One of her pages drew aside the silken curtains of the litter, and King Leodegrance gave her his hand. She stepped down, wrapped, as it were, in wonderful beauty. King Leodegrance led her to King Arthur, and King Arthur came to her. He placed one hand beneath her chin and the other upon her head, bent his face to hers, and kissed her smooth cheek. It was warm and fragrant, as soft as velvet, and without any blemish at all. When he had kissed her cheek, everyone there lifted up their voices in a great cheer, shouting for joy that those two noble souls had met.

In this way King Arthur welcomed the Lady Guinevere and her father, King Leodegrance, on the highway beneath the walls of the town of Camelot, about half a league away. No one who was there ever forgot that meeting, for it was full of extraordinary grace and noble courtesy.

Then King Arthur and his Court of Knights and nobles led King Leodegrance and the Lady Guinevere with great ceremony to Camelot and the royal castle. Rooms were given to everyone, and the whole place was alive with joy and beauty.
When high noon came, the whole Court went in great state and ceremony to the cathedral. There, surrounded by wonderful magnificence, those two noble souls were married by the Archbishop.

All the bells rang joyfully, and all the people who stood outside the cathedral shouted with loud cheers. And look! The King and the Queen came out shining, like the sun for splendor and like the moon for beauty.

In the castle a great noontime feast was laid out. At it sat four hundred and eighty-six lords and noble folk—kings, knights, and nobles—along with queens and ladies in magnificent dress. Near the King and the Queen sat King Leodegrance and Merlin, Sir Ulfius, Sir Ector the trustworthy, Sir Gawaine, Sir Ewaine, Sir Kay, King Ban, King Pellinore, and many other famous and honored people. No one had ever seen such magnificent courtliness as was seen at that famous wedding feast of King Arthur and Queen Guinevere.

That day was also very famous in the history of chivalry, for in the afternoon the famous Round Table was established. That Round Table was at once the very flower and the greatest glory of King Arthur’s reign.

About the middle of the afternoon, the King and Queen walked in procession, led by Merlin and followed by that whole splendid Court of kings, lords, nobles, and knights in full dress. They went to the place where Merlin, partly by magic and partly by skill, had caused a very wonderful pavilion to be built above the Round Table where it stood.

When the King and the Queen and the Court had gone inside, they were amazed at the beauty of the pavilion. It seemed to them a great space, like a marvelous land of the Fairies. The walls were richly gilded and painted with wonderful figures of saints and angels, dressed in deep blue and crimson. All those saints and angels were shown playing upon various musical instruments that seemed to be made of gold. Overhead, the roof of the pavilion was made to look like the sky, all sky-blue and sprinkled with stars. In the middle of that painted sky was an image of the sun in his glory. Underfoot was a pavement all of marble, set in squares of black and white, and blue and red, and several other colors.

In the middle of the pavilion stood a Round Table with seats for exactly fifty people. At each of the fifty places was a golden cup filled with fragrant wine, and a golden plate bearing a small loaf of fine white bread. When the King and his Court entered the pavilion, music suddenly began to play with wonderful sweetness.
Merlin now stepped up, grasped King Arthur’s hand, and drew him aside from Queen Guinevere. He said to the King, “Look, here stands the Round Table.”
Then King Arthur said, “Merlin, what I see is more wonderful than words can tell.”

After that, Merlin showed the King the various marvels of the Round Table. First he pointed to a tall seat, wonderfully carved from precious woods and gilded so that it was exceedingly beautiful. He said, “Behold, lord King, that seat is called the ‘Seat Royal,’ and it is yours to sit in.” As Merlin spoke, look! Letters of gold suddenly appeared on the back of that seat, and the golden letters spelled out the name,
ARTHUR, KING.

And Merlin said, “Lord, that seat may well be called the center seat of the Round Table, for truly you are the very center of all that is most worthy in true knighthood. So that seat shall be called the center seat of all the other seats.”

Then Merlin pointed to the seat that stood opposite the Seat Royal. That seat also looked very wonderful, as was told earlier in this history. And Merlin said to the King: “My lord King, that seat is called the Seat Perilous. Only one man in all the world may sit in it, and that man has not yet been born. If any other man dares to sit in it, he will either die or suffer a sudden and terrible misfortune for his boldness. That is why the seat is called the Seat Perilous.”

“Merlin,” said the King, “everything you tell me is beyond understanding, it is so marvelous. Now I beg you to find, with all speed, enough knights to fill this Round Table, so that my glory will be complete.”

Then Merlin smiled at the King, though not cheerfully, and said, “Lord, why are you in such a hurry? Know that when this Round Table is completely filled in all its seats, then your glory will be fully achieved, and right after that your day will begin to decline. For when any man has reached the crowning of his glory, his work is done, and God breaks him, as a man might break a cup from which such perfect wine has been drunk that no baser wine may be allowed to spoil it. So when your work is done and ended, God will shatter the cup of your life.”

Then the King looked very steadily into Merlin’s face and said, “Old man, what you say is always full of wonder, for you speak words of wisdom. Even so, since I am in God’s hands, I wish my glory and His good will to be accomplished, even if He then breaks me completely when I have served His purposes.”

“Lord,” said Merlin, “you speak like a worthy king and with a very large and noble heart. Even so, I cannot fill the Round Table for you at this time. Though you have gathered about you the noblest Court of Chivalry in all of Christendom, there are only thirty-two knights here who may be thought worthy to sit at the Round Table.”
“Then, Merlin,” said King Arthur, “I ask you to choose those thirty-two for me right now.”
“I will do so, lord King,” said Merlin.

Then Merlin looked around, and behold! He saw King Pellinore standing a little way off. Merlin went to him and took him by the hand. “Behold, my lord King,” he said. “Here is the knight in all the world who, next to yourself, is most worthy at this time to sit at this Round Table. He is very gentle in his manner toward the poor and needy, and at the same time so terribly strong and skillful that I do not know whether you or he would be more to be feared in a fight of knight against knight.”
Then Merlin led King Pellinore forward, and behold! Upon the high seat that stood to the left of the Royal Seat, a name suddenly appeared,
PELLINORE.

The name was blazoned in letters of gold that shone with extraordinary brightness. When King Pellinore took his seat, all those standing around gave him great and loud cheers that went on for a long time.

After Merlin had chosen King Arthur and King Pellinore in this way, he chose the following knights from King Arthur’s Court, thirty-two in all. These were the knights of great renown in chivalry who first established the Round Table. For this reason they were called “The Ancient and Honorable Companions of the Round Table.”

First there were Sir Gawaine and Sir Ewaine, who were the King’s nephews, and they sat near him on the right hand. There was Sir Ulfius (who held his seat only four years and eight months, until his death, after which Sir Geheris held that seat—he was squire to his brother, Sir Gawaine). There was Sir Kay the Seneschal, who was the King’s foster brother. There was Sir Baudwain of Britain (who held his seat only three years and two months, until his death, after which Sir Agravaine held that seat). There were Sir Pellias and Sir Geraint and Sir Constantine, son of Sir Caderes the Seneschal of Cornwall (who became king after King Arthur). There were Sir Caradoc and Sir Sagramore, called the Desirous, and Sir Dinadan and Sir Dodinas, called the Savage, and Sir Bruin, called the Black, and Sir Meliot of Logres. There were Sir Aglaval and Sir Durnure and Sir Lamorac (these three young knights were sons of King Pellinore). There were Sir Griflet and Sir Ladinas and Sir Brandiles and Sir Persavant of Ironside, and Sir Dinas of Cornwall, and Sir Brian of Listinoise. There were Sir Palomides and Sir Degraine and Sir Epinogres, the son of the King of North Umberland and brother of the enchantress Vivien. There were Sir Lamiel of Cardiff, and Sir Lucan the Bottler and his brother Sir Bedevere (who carried King Arthur to the ship of Fairies when he lay so badly wounded, close to death, after the last battle he fought). These thirty-two knights were the Ancient Companions of the Round Table. Others were added to them until there were forty-nine in all, and then Sir Galahad was added, and with him the Round Table was made completely full.
As Merlin chose each of these knights and took him by the hand, the knight’s name suddenly appeared in golden letters, very bright and shining, upon the seat that belonged to him.

But when all had been chosen, behold! King Arthur saw that the seat to the right of the Seat Royal had not been filled and had no name upon it. And he said to Merlin: “Merlin, how is it that the seat on my right hand has not been filled and has no name?”

And Merlin said: “Lord, there will be a name on it in a very little while. The one who sits in it will be the greatest knight in all the world, until the knight comes who will take the Seat Perilous. For the one who is coming will surpass all other men in beauty and in strength and in knightly grace.”
And King Arthur said: “I wish he were with us now.” And Merlin said: “He will come soon.”

So the Round Table was established with great pomp and ceremony. First the Archbishop of Canterbury blessed every seat, moving from place to place with his Holy Court around him. The choir sang most sweetly together, while others swung censers from which rose a wonderfully fragrant smoke of frankincense, filling the whole pavilion with a scent of Heavenly blessedness.

When the Archbishop had blessed every one of those seats, each chosen knight took his place at the Round Table. His squire came and stood behind him, holding the small banner with his coat of arms on the point of a spear above the knight’s head. And all those who stood about that place, both knights and ladies, lifted up their voices in loud cheers.

Then all the knights rose. Each knight held up the cross of his sword’s hilt in front of him, and each one repeated every word that King Arthur spoke. This was the covenant of their Knighthood of the Round Table. They promised to be gentle to the weak and brave against the strong. They promised to be terrible to the wicked and to anyone who did evil. They promised to defend the helpless who called on them for aid, and to hold all women sacred. They promised to stand up for one another whenever that help was needed, and to be merciful to all people. They promised to be kind in their deeds, true in friendship, and faithful in love. This was their covenant, and each knight swore to it on the cross of his sword. As a witness to his oath, he kissed the hilt. Then everyone standing nearby cheered loudly once more.

Then all the knights of the Round Table sat down. Each knight broke bread from the golden plate and drank wine from the golden cup that stood before him. They gave thanks to God for the food and drink they were having.
So King Arthur was married to Queen Guinevere, and so the Round Table was founded.
